content: Write a letter of recommendation for an employee applying for an internal promotion.

**[Company Name / Letterhead]**
[Street Address]
[City, State ZIP]

[Date]

[Recipient Name]
[Recipient Title]
[Department]
[Company Name]

**Re: Recommendation for [Employee Name] — [Target Position Title], Req. #[XXXX]**

Dear [Mr./Ms./Dr. Last Name or Hiring Committee],

I am writing to offer my strongest recommendation for [Employee Name]'s promotion to [Target Position Title]. I have had the pleasure of working with [Employee First Name] for [number] years as [his/her/their] [direct manager / team lead / cross-functional partner] in the [Department] group, and in that time [he/she/they] [has/have] consistently performed at a level that exceeds the expectations of [his/her/their] current role. In my view, this promotion would formalize responsibilities [Employee First Name] has already begun to shoulder.

[Employee First Name] joined our team in [Month, Year] as a [Current Title], and the trajectory since has been remarkable. Among [his/her/their] most significant contributions:

- **[Achievement 1]** — [e.g., Led the migration of our client onboarding process to the new platform, reducing average onboarding time from 14 days to 5 and eliminating roughly 200 hours of manual work per quarter.]
- **[Achievement 2]** — [e.g., Owned the quarterly forecasting model, improving accuracy from ±12% to ±4% and giving leadership meaningfully better visibility into pipeline risk.]
- **[Achievement 3]** — [e.g., Mentored three junior analysts, two of whom have since been promoted, and built the training documentation now used department-wide.]

Beyond results, what distinguishes [Employee First Name] is [his/her/their] judgment. [He/She/They] [is/are] the person colleagues seek out when a problem is ambiguous, because [he/she/they] ask[s] the right questions before proposing solutions and [is/are] candid about tradeoffs rather than telling people what they want to hear. During [specific challenging period or project — e.g., the Q3 vendor transition], [he/she/they] kept a stressed cross-functional team aligned and communicated proactively with stakeholders at every level, including [senior leader or client name/type].

The [Target Position Title] role calls for [key requirement 1, e.g., managing a team of five] and [key requirement 2, e.g., owning the departmental budget]. [Employee First Name] has already demonstrated capability in both areas: [brief evidence, e.g., informally leading a three-person workstream since January and co-managing a $1.2M project budget without a single overrun]. I am confident [he/she/they] would step into the expanded scope with a short ramp-up.

To be balanced, [Employee First Name] and I have discussed [growth area — e.g., delegating more readily rather than absorbing work personally], and [he/she/they] [has/have] made deliberate progress on it over the past [timeframe] — a sign of the coachability that makes me confident in [his/her/their] continued growth at the next level.

Losing [Employee First Name] from my team would be a real cost to our group, and I recommend [him/her/them] anyway, because [he/she/they] [has/have] earned this and the organization will be better for it. Please feel free to contact me at [phone] or [email] if I can provide further detail.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]
[Your Title]
[Department] | [Company Name]
[Phone] | [Email]

---

**A few tips for adapting this:**
- **Quantify at least two accomplishments.** Numbers ("cut cycle time 40%") are far more persuasive than adjectives ("hardworking").
- **Map to the job description.** Pull two or three requirements from the posting and give direct evidence for each — internal committees screen for exactly this.
- **Include one honest growth area with evidence of improvement.** It makes the praise credible; pure superlatives read as boilerplate.
- **Address the "backfill" question if you're the current manager.** Signaling that you support the move despite the cost to your own team carries real weight.

If you share the employee's actual accomplishments and the role details, I'm happy to draft a fully specific version.
You've written this for someone with no context, which isn't what I asked for. Rewrite it for a reader who already knows the background.

**Re: [Employee Name] — [Target Position Title], Req. #[XXXX]**

Dear [Name],

I'm writing in support of [Employee Name] for [Target Position Title]. You know [his/her/their] work, so I'll skip the résumé and speak to the question actually in front of the committee: whether [he/she/they] can operate at this level now.

I think the answer is yes, and I'd point to three things.

First, [he/she/they] [has/have] been doing a meaningful share of this job since [month]. [Specific example — e.g., the [Project] workstream has effectively been hers since Q1; I've been in the status meetings as a courtesy, not a necessity.] The scope change here is real but not a leap.

Second, judgment under pressure. [Specific example — e.g., during the vendor transition, when the timeline collapsed, she came to me with two options and a recommendation rather than a problem, and she was right about which risk mattered.] That instinct — knowing what to escalate and what to simply handle — is the part of this role that's hardest to teach, and it's already there.

Third, [he/she/they] [is/are] trusted laterally. [Specific example — e.g., Finance and Ops both route questions to her directly now, which was not true a year ago and didn't happen by accident.] For a role that runs on influence more than authority, that matters more than any single deliverable.

On the open question I expect you'll raise: [growth area — e.g., delegation]. It's fair. [He/She/They] [has/have] historically absorbed work rather than distributing it, and we've talked about it directly. [Evidence of change — e.g., she's handed off two of her recurring deliverables since June and has been deliberate about coaching rather than correcting.] I'd want [his/her/their] first quarter in the role to include explicit support on [specific — e.g., headcount planning], which [he/she/they] [hasn't/haven't] touched yet. That's a ramp-up need, not a reservation.

Backfilling [him/her/them] will hurt my team, and I'd still make this move. [He/She/They] [has/have] outgrown the current role, and keeping [him/her/them] in it is the more expensive option.

Happy to talk further if it's useful.

[Your Name]
[Your Title]

---

The brackets are placeholders for the details I don't have. Give me the actual projects, the growth area, and the role's real requirements and I'll write it straight through.
This runs much longer than it needed to and buries the point. Cut it to about half the length and lead with the main point.

**Re: [Employee Name] — [Target Position Title], Req. #[XXXX]**

Dear [Name],

[Employee Name] should get this role. [He/She/They] [has/have] been doing much of it since [month] — [specific example, e.g., the [Project] workstream has been hers in practice; I attend status meetings as a courtesy, not a necessity] — and the promotion would mostly formalize what's already true.

Two things convince me it holds at the next level. [He/She/They] escalate[s] the right things and handle[s] the rest: [brief example, e.g., when the vendor timeline collapsed, she brought me two options and a recommendation, and was right about which risk mattered]. And [he/she/they] [is/are] trusted laterally — [brief example, e.g., Finance and Ops now route questions to her directly, which wasn't true a year ago].

On [growth area, e.g., delegation]: fair concern, and we've discussed it. [Evidence, e.g., she's handed off two recurring deliverables since June.] [He/She/They] will need support on [specific gap, e.g., headcount planning] in the first quarter. Ramp-up need, not a reservation.

Backfilling [him/her/them] will hurt my team. I'd still make the move — keeping [him/her/them] in the current role is the more expensive option.

[Your Name]
[Your Title]
